sm: Albert Mohler opens by quoting Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called Tuesday's election an extinction level event for Republicans. He cites a New York Times headline that every major demographic group swung left, with a fifteen point shift among all voters, thirteen among white voters, twenty-eight among Hispanic voters, seventeen among Asian voters, and nine among black voters. Young voters moved more than thirty points, and young men nearly forty points toward Democrats after a twenty-three point move toward Republicans in 2024. Mohler says many young men are frustrated that the job and education worlds are not working, and that frustration now points at Republicans, partly over the Iran war and the economy. He adds that Democrats will have a commanding House majority and that Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek Republican leadership.

Mohler says Republicans now face the disadvantages of minority status, and that Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become Speaker while some Democratic senators-elect say they will not back Chuck Schumer as leader. As a Christian, he worries some will push the Republican Party left on transgender issues, LGBTQ issues and abortion, where he says there is no middle ground. He names DeSantis, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as possible leaders. Vance publicly blamed the Iran war for the losses, and President Trump said that might be right but that the action is worth it if it stops Iran getting a nuclear weapon. He then turns to headlines about a religious left revival, noting that seven to nine Democratic winners were identified with mainline Protestantism, including Senators-elect James Talarico of Texas and Adam Hamilton of Kansas.

Mohler notes that Kansas had not elected a Democratic senator in about ninety years and Texas not in a generation. Hamilton is the founding pastor of the large United Methodist Church of the Resurrection, and Mohler says he has helped move the denomination left and push conservatives out. Talarico is a young, unmarried seminarian at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, and both won because of their liberal religious identity, not in spite of it. Mohler says liberal theology tries to make peace between a secular worldview and historic Christianity, while conservatives hold to the faith once delivered to the saints. He recalls liberals in the early twentieth century denying the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection and the authority of Scripture, and says Hamilton is cagey but solidly liberal. He suggests public persona helped them, and begins contrasting Talarico with Republican Ken Paxton.

Mohler says many evangelical pastors could not support either a liberal Democrat or Ken Paxton, whom even Trump found unlikable, while Talarico seems like the kid next door. His lesson for Republicans is that likability is not enough on its own, but its absence is fatal, especially in the age of smartphones and TikTok. He says the religious left is back at least electorally, though not necessarily in church attendance, and that liberal Protestantism has long been more explicitly political and has reduced the gospel to social action. He predicts Senate clashes between conservative Christians and liberal Protestants. He closes with a story about hackers using artificial intelligence to raise freezer temperatures in European grocery stores, ruining millions of dollars of food, helped by a default password of one two three four five. The episode ends with a pitch for his new book on Western civilization, available for pre-order, and his usual sign-off links.
